Where it began

Dwayne Bravo was born on 7 October 1983 in Santa Cruz. He first played for Trinidad and Tobago in 2002, against Barbados, opening the batting and not getting a bowl. A first-class hundred followed only a month later.

It was the ball that made people sit up. In early 2003 he took 6 for 11 against the Windward Islands, and from then on he was seen as a genuine all-rounder.

The player

His Test career began at Lord's in 2004, with 44 and 10 and three wickets. He finished that series in England with 16 wickets and 220 runs. At Old Trafford he top-scored with 77 in the first innings and then took 6 for 55, which stood as his best Test bowling. His first Test hundred, 107, came against South Africa in Antigua in 2005. Later that year in Hobart he made 113, his highest Test score, after arriving with West Indies in a tight spot, and in the next Test, at Adelaide, he took 6 for 84.

He played 40 Tests between 2004 and 2010, scoring 2,200 runs at 31.43 with three hundreds and 13 fifties, and taking 86 wickets at 39.70. He held 38 catches.

What made him special

Bravo was a lively hitter in the lower order and a clever bowler at the end of an innings, known for slower yorkers that fooled good batters. He was part of the West Indies sides that won the 2004 Champions Trophy and the World Twenty20 titles of 2012 and 2016, and in 2012 he took the catch that won the final. In 2020 he became the first bowler to reach 500 wickets in T20 cricket.

He was rarely dull. At Old Trafford in 2007 he took the gloves for a while as emergency wicketkeeper, and in the same match a bouncer of his knocked Kevin Pietersen's helmet onto the stumps, out hit wicket. If there was a weakness, the figures hint at it: 71 Test innings and only one not out. Hanging about at the end was not really his game.

Away from the middle

Music was the other half of the story. He launched a single, Chalo Chalo, in Chennai in 2015, and in 2016 he released Champion to celebrate the World Twenty20 win. It went to the top of the charts in India.

In the Indian Premier League he was the first player to win the Purple Cap twice, in 2013 and 2015, and his 32 wickets in 2013 were a record for a single season at the time. He kept playing T20 cricket around the world until September 2024. He then turned to coaching, first as bowling coach at Chennai Super Kings and then, from 2025, as mentor at Kolkata Knight Riders.

And finally

Most cricketers mark a world title with a lap of the ground. Bravo marked his with a song, and India sang along.
